Assignment 1 -- Insights from Overwatch League¶

76 total marks¶

In [330]:
# You will need the following packages
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
import numpy as np

Introduction¶

Business Context. You work for Overwatch League, the premier esports league for the game Overwatch. They have collected data about past pro tournaments and would like you to answer some questions about past tournaments. Build visualizations and answer the questions below.

About Overwatch League. In the Overwatch League, teams of professional players compete against each other to be the best in the world at playing the team-based first-person shooter game, Overwatch.

Each match consists of two teams of six players each, with each player selecting one of the game's many heroes to play as. The teams are then tasked with completing various objectives, such as escorting a payload across the map or capturing and holding control points.

The team that is able to complete their objectives the quickest or prevent the other team from completing their objectives wins the match.

Matches are typically played in a best-of-three format, meaning that the first team to win two rounds is declared the winner. Each round is called a "map", and the team that wins the most maps wins the match.

The Overwatch League is divided into two seasons per year, with teams from all around the world competing in a variety of different venues. The top teams from each season advance to the playoffs, where they compete for the chance to be crowned the Overwatch League champion. Each map is one of two types, it is either a control map or an escort map.

Business Problem. Your task is to format the given data and provide visualizations that would answer the specific questions the client has, which are mentioned below.

  • Analytical Context. You are given a CSV file (stored in the already created data folder) containing details about each match like winning team, map type, date of match, tournament title, etc. You will be performing the following tasks on the data:
  1. Read, transform, and prepare data for visualization
  2. Perform analytics and construct visualizations of the data to identify patterns in the dataset

The client has a specific set of questions they would like to get answers to. You will need to provide visualizations to accompany these.

We have the following columns

  • round_start_time Stating time of the round
  • round_end_time Ending time of the round
  • stage Stage of the competition
  • match_id Id for the match
  • game_number Game number in the given match
  • match_winner Winner of the match
  • map_winner Winner of the game/map
  • map_loser Lost of the game/map
  • map_name Name of map

  • winning_team_final_map_score Final score of map winner
  • losing_team_final_map_score Final score of map loser
  • control_round_name Name of the round if it was a control type map
  • attacker Team that was the attacker

  • team_one_name Name of first team in match
  • team_two_name Name of second team in match
  • attacker_payload_distance Distance the attacker moved the payload on payload maps
  • defender_payload_distance
  • attacker_time_banked Attacker time left over
  • defender_time_banked Defender time left over
  • attacker_control_perecent Percent objective was charged by the attacker team
  • defender_control_perecent Percent objective was charged by the defender team

Question 2 -- Cleaning the data (5 marks)¶

In this dataset there are two types of maps, escort and control. On control maps, the teams try to control an objective until the meter reaches 100. On escort maps, the attacker tries to escort a payload to the end of the map, while the defender tries to stop it. Control maps can be found in the dataset by rows where the control_perecent is not 0 for at least one team. That is, control_perecent will be Nan or 0 for both teams when the map is not a control map.

Rules¶

  • If control_percent for at least one of the teams > 0 --> control map
  • If control_percent for both teams = 0 or NaN --> escort map

# get unique teams from team_one_name and team_two_name

team_two_name = df.team_two_name.unique()

teams = list(team_one_name)

# for loop to add in unique team names from team_two_name

  • 3d) (5 marks) Make a horizontal bar chart displaying the win rate on control maps of each team, order the bar chart from lowest win rate to highest win rate, add a vertical line at 50%. Color the teams by country. Hint it is useful to use the sns.barplot function, set the dodge argument as follows:dodge=False and make use of the orient, hue and hue_order arguements.
In [344]:
# win_rate = number of games won / number of games played (use map winner)

# create empty lists
data_win_rate = []

# create DataFrame from country dictionary
win_rate_control = pd.DataFrame.from_dict(country)

for team in teams:
    
    # count wins for the team
    team_wins = len(df_control_maps[df_control_maps["map_winner"] == team])
    print(f"{team} Wins: {team_wins}")

    # count total games played (both as winner or loser)
    total_games_played = len(df_control_maps[(df_control_maps["map_winner"] == team) | (df_control_maps["map_loser"] == team)])
    print(f"{team} Total Games Played: {total_games_played}")

    # calculate win_rate
    if total_games_played > 0: # avoid division by zero
        win_rate = team_wins / total_games_played
    else:
        win_rate = 0
    print(f"{team} Win Rate: {win_rate}")
    print()

    # append win rate
    data_win_rate.append(win_rate)

# add win rate column to DataFrame
win_rate_control["win rate"] = data_win_rate
    
win_rate_control

# create an empty list to store results
win_rate_yearly_data = []

# convert country dictionary into a lookup dictionary
country_lookup = dict(zip(country["team names"], country["country"]))

# iterate through each year in the control maps DataFrame
for year in df_control_maps["year"].unique():

    # filter the DataFrame for the current year
    yearly_data = df_control_maps[df_control_maps["year"] == year]

    # iterate through each team in the teams list
    for team in teams:

        # find country name based on lookup dictionary
        country_name = country_lookup.get(team)

        # count total wins in a given year
        team_wins_yearly = len(yearly_data[yearly_data["map_winner"] == team])
                           
        # count total games played (both as winner or loser) in a given year
        total_games_played_yearly = len(yearly_data[(yearly_data["map_winner"] == team) | (yearly_data["map_loser"] == team)])

        # calculate win_rate
        if total_games_played_yearly > 0: # avoid division by zero
            win_rate_yearly = team_wins_yearly / total_games_played_yearly
        else:
            win_rate_yearly = 0

        # append results in a dictionary
        win_rate_yearly_data.append({
            "year": year,
            "team": team,
            "country": country_name,
            "win rate yearly": win_rate_yearly
        })

# create DataFrame
win_rate_control_by_year = pd.DataFrame(win_rate_yearly_data)
win_rate_control_by_year

  • 5b) (5 marks) Which plot should be used to make recommendations for Toronto in 2023? Based on this judgement and the plot you generated, what map should Toronto practice the most? Are there any problems with this analysis?

The plot for 2022 should be used to make recommendations for Toronto in 2023 as it will provide the most recent data on performance, highlighting current areas of strength and weakness. Furthermore, older data may not accurately reflect the strategies and dynamics of the current team members, affecting its application for future recommendations.

Based on this reasoning, Toronto should practice the Well control map since they performed poorly on that map in 2022. This round map had the lowest win rate at around 0.4.

One issue with the analysis is that the graph does not provide information on sample size. By looking at this graph, we cannot determine how many rounds were played on each map, making it difficult to determine the reliability of the win rates. For example, a low win rate on a given control map with few plays could be due to random variance as opposed to true weakness. Including sample sizes would provide better context and allow for more informed recommendations.

  • 5c) (2 marks) Assign each team a rank according to their 2022 control map win rate, with 1 being the highest win rate on control maps in 2022 and 20 being the lowest win rate on control maps in 2022. Print each team name with its rank beside it.
In [364]:
# subset 2022 control map data
df_control_2022 = df_control_maps[df_control_maps["year"] == 2022]

# calculate the number of wins for each team
team_wins_2022 = df_control_2022.groupby("map_winner").size().reset_index(name="wins")

# calculate total games played (winner and loser)
total_games_2022 = (
    pd.concat([df_control_2022["map_winner"], df_control_2022["map_loser"]])
    .value_counts()
    .reset_index(name="total_games")
)

# rename column in DataFrame
total_games_2022 = total_games_2022.rename(columns = {"index": "team"})
team_wins_2022 = team_wins_2022.rename(columns = {"map_winner": "team"})

# merge two DataFrames
team_stats_2022 = pd.merge(team_wins_2022, total_games_2022, left_on = "team", right_on= "team", how = "outer")

# calculate win rate
team_stats_2022["win_rate"] = team_stats_2022["wins"] / team_stats_2022["total_games"]

# assign rank based on win rate
team_stats_2022["rank"] = team_stats_2022["win_rate"].rank(ascending = False, method = "dense").astype(int)

# sort teams by rank
team_stats_2022_sorted = team_stats_2022.sort_values(by = "rank")

# Print sorted results
teams_2022 = list(team_stats_2022_sorted["team"])
ranks_2022 = list(team_stats_2022_sorted["rank"])

for i in range(len(teams_2022)):
    team = teams_2022[i]
    rank = ranks_2022[i]
    print(f"{rank}. {team}")

for map_name in maps_of_interest:

    # filter the DataFrame for the map of interest
    map_data = df_control_2022[df_control_2022["control_round_name"] == map_name]

    # list opponents whether Toronto was a winner/loser
    opponent = list(map_data.loc[map_data["map_winner"] == "Toronto Defiant", "map_loser"])
    opponent += list(map_data.loc[map_data["map_loser"] == "Toronto Defiant", "map_winner"])

    # calculate mean rank of opponents
    if len(opponent) > 0:

        # filter main DataFrame to get ranks
        opponent_ranks = team_stats_2022[team_stats_2022["team"].isin(opponent)]["rank"]

        # calculate mean rank
        mean_rank = opponent_ranks.mean()

    else:
        mean_rank = None

    mean_ranks[map_name] = mean_rank

for map_name, mean_rank in mean_ranks.items():
    category = "Worst" if map_name in worst else "Best"
    print(f"Mean rank of teams Toronto played on the {category} map '{map_name}: {mean_rank}")

  • 5e) (3 marks) Compare the mean ranks on Toronto's best maps to their worst maps. What does this analysis reveal about Toronto's map-specific win rates?

The mean ranks of opponents on Toronto's best maps vary significantly - Toronto beat top-ranked team on MEKA base (average rank = 1) whereas they beat mid-ranked teams on Shrine (averge rank = 14). On the other hand, Toronto seemed to beat only-average-ranked teams on their worst maps (Well, University, Garden). Overall, given the large variability in ranks Toronto faced, it suggests that the Toronto team has map-specific strengths and weaknesses. More specifically, Toronto has strategic and/or tactical strengths on the MEKA Base and Sanctuary map.

Question 7 -- (8 marks)¶

On escort maps, the attacker must push a "payload" a certain distance within an alotted time. If the attacker pushes the payload to the end of the map before the alotted time is up, then the attacker can bank that time. On the other hand, if the attacker does not push the payload to the end of the map, the distance they were able to push it is recorded.

  • 7b) (4 marks) Describe the characteristics of the histrograms and interpret the summary statistics in the context of the data.

Histogram 1 Analyis¶

The histogram has a right-skewed distribution with many 0 values indicating that there were many cases where attackers won right as time ran out. This suggests that escort maps could be challenging to complete with a lot of time left. On average, attacker teams finished with around 102 seconds banked. And the most time an attacker team has banked was 404 seconds. There seems to be significant variation in how efficiently terams can complete maps.

Histogram 2 Analyis¶

The histogram has a right-skewed distribution with many 0 values indicating that there were many cases where attackers failed to push the payload at all before losing the round. On average, attacker teams moved the payload 44 units before losing. And the maximum payload an attacker team has moved was 127 units.
